    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40654v1</id>
    <title>Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40654v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40654v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private.
  We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations.
  We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40652v1</id>
    <title>Reconstructing hidden observables via quantum snapshot thermometry</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40652v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40652v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Projective snapshots are a standard readout tool for quantum simulators, but they directly probe only observables that are diagonal in the measurement basis. We show how local equilibration and an independently calibrated equilibrium equation of state can reveal otherwise hidden conserved-density profiles. We demonstrate numerically that such ``quantum snapshot thermometry'' can recover energy fronts and a diffusion constant, distinguish spin transport from energy spreading, and reveal conserved-charge profiles invisible in the initial measurements. We also identify symmetry-imposed ambiguities in the readout and show how prior knowledge of the spatial structure can resolve them. Fixed-basis snapshot thermometry thus provides quantitative hydrodynamic information beyond transport exponents, bypassing additional measurement bases and quantum state tomography.</summary>

    <title>Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:33Z</updated>

    <summary>Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove stability of the asynchronous \textsf{R} squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.</summary>

    <title>Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40649v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40649v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions.
  This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.</summary>

    <title>Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40647v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40647v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.</summary>

    <title>Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:59:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40644v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40644v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.</summary>

    <updated>2026-10-29T17:58:59Z</updated>

    <summary>Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.</summary>

    <summary>Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates.     <title>Entanglement diagnostics of stochastic-resetting steady states: theory and measurement on superconducting qubits</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:58:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40638v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Stochastic resetting drives quantum systems into nonequilibrium stationary states unreachable under uninterrupted unitary evolution, and their entanglement depends on whether the reset history is resolved or averaged over. We study this interplay in the transverse-field Ising chain, deriving closed-form results for two qubits and evaluating chains of up to 12 qubits exactly. In the two-qubit system, these closed-form results show that phase matching between energy eigenstates produces resonances, and their visibility in the stationary state is determined by the symmetry of the reset state. Measurements on an IBM superconducting processor show the entropies evaluated before and after the reset average closely following noiseless predictions with no fitted parameter, while concurrence lies below prediction across most of the hardware measurements. The two diagnostics respond differently because they read different components of the same reconstructed state, and a depolarizing model captures the concurrence suppression with one fitted parameter. The difference between the two entropies, i. e., the Jensen gap of entanglement entropy, equals the Holevo information that a subsystem retains about the time since the last reset. With a Bell-state reset, this information grows with chain length across a half-chain cut over the sizes studied, without visible saturation at the smaller reset probabilities. Since reset times are sampled and recorded classically, the trajectory-averaged entropy, and with it the Jensen gap, is obtained without postselection, in contrast to monitored circuits, where trajectory-resolved entanglement requires sampling exponentially rare measurement records.</summary>

    <title>Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:58:16Z</updated>

    <summary>An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.</summary>

    <summary>Can the ground state of a local Hamiltonian be prepared by local dissipation? We address this question for free-fermion Hamiltonians, using a quadratic Lindbladian with linear jump operators for the dissipative ground-state preparation. For translation-invariant targets, Fourier correspondence relates spatial locality to momentum-space analyticity, allowing us to derive a complete spectral criterion for the existence of exponentially local linear jump operators that prepare the ground state. This criterion leads to a no-go theorem that, sign-changing Fermi-level crossings exclude exponentially local linear jump operators for preparing the ground state. While these crossings are the complete obstruction in one dimension, additional obstructions generally arise in higher dimensions. We illustrate these additional obstructions using two quadratic-band-touching models with algebraically decaying ground-state correlations. We further show that short-range ground-state correlations, although not necessary, are sufficient for local dissipative preparation even without translation invariance. Our results establish how the spectral structure of the target Hamiltonian governs the locality of dissipative ground-state preparation.</summary>

    <summary>Left-handed (LH) superconducting transmission lines, built with series capacitors and shunt inductors instead of the series inductors and shunt capacitors of a conventional right-handed (RH) line, have a spectrum with a nonzero lower band edge and modes that become sparse at high frequencies. We study the dynamical Casimir effect in a LH line terminated by a flux-modulated SQUID and compare it with an RH line built from the same elements and with a long coplanar waveguide terminated by the same SQUID. We derive the quantum Hamiltonian and show that the coupling between two modes factorizes into their amplitudes at the SQUID. Together, the LH spectrum and the mode dependence of this coupling determine which modes are populated and how fast. With equal elements, the LH coupling grows with frequency and exceeds the RH one above a crossover pump frequency set by the cell inductance and capacitance, and only the LH line has resonances above the RH band edge. Pumping two modes at once lets a weakly coupled mode borrow coupling from a strongly coupled one, while crossings of resonance lines populate three or four modes without increasing the growth rate. Compared with the coplanar waveguide, the LH line has a similar coupling but keeps the created particles in the target mode, whereas the nearly equidistant waveguide spreads them over many pairs and needs more pump energy.</summary>

    <title>An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:55:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.</summary>

    <title>Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:54:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40616v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40616v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model's training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image's difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model's own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as $x$-, $v$-, and $ε$-prediction models. Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC.</summary>

    <title>TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:54:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40613v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40613v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.</summary>

    <title>Exceptional Points as Witnesses of Non-Gaussian Noise</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:54:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40612v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40612v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Efficient control of quantum devices requires the knowledge of their environmental noise, yet the commonly measured power spectrum does not fully characterize non-Gaussian fluctuations of realistic environments. Here we show that exceptional points (EPs) in the noise-averaged dephasing response can expose observable signatures of non-Gaussian statistics, distinguishing environments with identical lower-order statistics. We also introduce a theoretical model that describes dephasing environments in terms of identical independent noise sources while preserving the power spectrum. Given a calibrated single-source model, the largest EP order extracted from the measured dephasing response determines the number of sources and predicts the higher-order statistics of the combined noise. We illustrate an atomtronic readout that maps distinct EP signatures onto an evolving ensemble-averaged atomic interference pattern. Our results connect non-Hermitian dynamics to environmental noise statistics, providing a route to characterize noise in quantum devices used in computing, metrology, and precision measurement.</summary>

    <title>When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:54:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40611v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40611v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40596v1</id>
    <title>Algebraic theory of abelian fractons and beyond</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:50:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40596v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40596v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We develop an algebraic theory of fusion, mobility, and statistics in abelian gapped fracton orders and topological phases. The framework generalizes the algebraic description of abelian anyons to systems with restricted-mobility and spatially extended excitations. We consider translation-invariant bosonic systems whose pointlike and extended excitations have finite fusion order. The basic objects are braided fusion complexes (BFCs): chain complexes encoding fusion and mobility, equipped with a braiding chain map encoding statistics. Their equivalence classes define braided fusion theories (BFTs). Our framework encompasses arbitrary translation-invariant Pauli codes, as well as all abelian anyon theories in two spatial dimensions, including chiral theories. We give evidence for the conjecture that every nondegenerate BFT can be realized as the excitation theory of a gapped phase and that the BFT describing such a phase is a phase invariant. We derive constraints on pointlike fusion and mobility, showing, for example, that neither the Pauli X nor Z sectors of the X-cube and anisotropic models can occur alone in a nondegenerate BFT. For nondegenerate theories with only pointlike excitations, we extract a simpler theory of mutual statistics, consisting of a fusion module and a map to its statistical dual. This theory of mutual statistics is an invariant of the BFT and, at odd fusion order, gives an equivalent description of the full braided fusion theory. We interpret remote detection as the generalization of mutual statistics to fracton orders. In the BFC setting, we give a precise formulation of the excitation-detector principle: every nontrivial excitation can be detected by an operator supported at spatial infinity, and every nontrivial detector detects some excitation. Assuming a unique infinite-space ground state, we prove that this principle is equivalent to nondegeneracy.</summary>

    <title>Optimal detuning and gate time for strongly driven single-qubit gates beyond the rotating-wave approximation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:49:56Z</updated>

    <summary>Single-qubit quantum gates are implemented as the time-controlled unitary evolution of a two-level system under harmonic driving. The rotating-wave approximation (RWA) provides closed-form gate parameters for weak coupling. Larger amplitudes, desirable to speed up the dynamics, make the RWA-designed gates inaccurate because of the neglected counter-rotating term, which also shifts the resonance (Bloch-Siegert shift). By detuning the driving frequency by an amplitude-dependent shift of Bloch-Siegert type and rescaling the operation time, the RWA gate conditions are recovered with corrected parameters. Numerical solutions of the Schrodinger equation show that these corrections lower the gate infidelity by several orders of magnitude, extending the range of usable amplitudes</summary>

    <title>Probing fluctuations in photon emission statistics of spin injected quantum dots with time dependent electronic excitation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:49:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40593v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40593v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Electrically spin-injected ensembles of InGaAs/GaAs quantum dots emit circularly polarized single photons, with the emission helicity determined by the spin polarization of the injected electrons. A ferromagnetic CoFeB spin-injection layer with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, combined with an MgO tunnel barrier, enables spin-polarized electron injection into the quantum-dot active region, resulting in circularly polarized photon emission at zero applied magnetic field. These devices realize direct spin-charge-photon conversion in an electrically driven, microelectronics-compatible quantum light source that operates without an external pump laser. Using an extended Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer with four detectors and time-tagged readout, we measure time-resolved photon-number statistics that resolve up to $|2\rangle$ Fock states within a single excitation cycle. While single-photon ($n=|1\rangle$) emission tracks the electrical excitation pulse as expected, the two-photon ($n=|2\rangle$) statistics exhibit pronounced fluctuations at multiple temporal positions within the pulse. These fluctuations vanish upon demagnetization of the spin-injection layer, establishing a direct link between the multi-photon emission dynamics and the spin polarization of the injected carriers. The observations indicate that spin injection controls not only the helicity of the emitted photons but also higher-order temporal correlations of the emission. The behavior is phenomenologically captured by inserting both a variable excitation mechanism and a set of multi-emitter collapse operators within a stochastic wave function evolution. The platform thus opens a route to electrically driven, spin-controlled single and multi-photon Fock-state sources and provides a testbed for spin-conditioned multi-emitter dynamics in solid-state quantum light sources.</summary>

    <title>Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:49:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40592v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40592v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.</summary>

    <title>Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:47:50Z</updated>

    <summary>An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.</summary>

    <title>Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:47:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40588v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator's rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent's activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm.</summary>

    <summary>Can entangling codewords across independent uses of a quantum channel improve the rate of classical communication? An old conjecture states that there is no such entanglement advantage for all channels. Although Hastings's result and follow-up works disproved this conjecture, it turns out that enormous dimension is required to construct a channel where entanglement enhances classical communication. This indicates that there might be no entanglement advantage for many physical channels, or for all low dimensional channels. Motivated by recent progress on (generalized) amplitude damping channels, we propose a general Schur-weighted block entropy inequality, and show that there is no entanglement advantage for all phase-covariant channels including multi-level amplitude damping channels, generalized dephasing channels, and damping-dephasing channels. As a by-product, we also recover the recently established result that there is no entanglement advantage for all qubit channels.</summary>

    <title>VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:45:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40578v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40578v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.</summary>

    <title>What Can Be Computed with Indefinite Causal Structure?</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:44:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40573v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40573v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Can quantum computation become more powerful when operations do not need to follow a definite causal order? We study this question in the process matrix formalism of Oreshkov et al. (Nature Communications, 2012), which allows quantum operations to be connected without a fixed global order. In the computational model, a quantum circuit succinctly describes a process matrix, and the algorithm is given access to its generated channel, with computational cost measured by the size of the generating circuit.
  We give polynomial-time algorithms in two settings. First, general process matrix computation suffices to solve every problem in $\textbf{NP}$. The valid processes used by our algorithm satisfy the purification postulate of Araújo et al. (Quantum, 2017), and their generated channels are unitary, although their generating circuits are not. Second, requiring the process matrices themselves to be pure, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for unique-sink orientation, a general problem capturing several longstanding computational problems in optimization. Our unitary generators are constructed explicitly and efficiently. Assuming that unique-sink orientation has no quantum polynomial-time algorithm, our result shows that indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond $\textbf{BQP}$ within the process matrix formalism, even while preserving unitarity.</summary>

    <title>On the Quantum Chromatic Gap II</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:44:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40571v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40571v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We confirm a conjecture of the first author [SODA'26] on a strong form of pseudo-telepathy for Khot's $d$-to-$1$ games: for every $d\geq 4$, every $ε>0$, and every $k\in\mathbb N$, there is a $d$-to-$1$ label-cover game of classical value less than $ε$ that admits a perfect quantum strategy using finite-dimensional shared entanglement with measurement contexts of radius at least $k$. As a consequence, there exist graphs whose quantum chromatic number $χ_q$ is $3$ and whose classical chromatic number $χ$ is arbitrarily large. This is the first improvement on the quantum chromatic gap since the work of Brassard, Cleve, and Tapp [Phys. Rev. Lett.'99], which produced graphs for which $χ$ grows exponentially in $χ_q$.
  To prove the conjecture, we proceed as follows. We start with a ``stretched'' version of the Mermin--Peres magic square, obtained by spacing out its equations and linking them with additional long equation wires. This operation increases the radius of the initial measurement contexts of a perfect quantum strategy for the game, while preserving classical unsatisfiability. We then apply parallel repetition to make the classical value small, and we turn the system into a pseudo-telepathic multi-layered Kneser hypergraph via a PCP construction of Dinur, Guruswami, Khot, and Regev [STOC'03]. Finally, we feed the resulting hypergraph into the reduction of Fei, Minzer, and Wang from hypergraph colouring to $4$-to-$1$ games, we establish quantum completeness of this reduction, and we show that it preserves context radius.</summary>

    <title>Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:43:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40567v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40567v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Coherent noise can give rise to unconventional regimes of quantum information recovery and mixed-state order. We study these phenomena in two settings related by Wegner duality: the triangular-lattice surface code subject to single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ rotations followed by syndrome measurements, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ paramagnet subject to strongly symmetric decoherence. Increasing the rotation angle drives a transition from a decodable phase to a \emph{partially decodable} critical phase in the code, and from a strongly symmetric phase to a phase with \emph{algebraic} $\mathbb{Z}_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in the dual paramagnet. We develop a common description of these phenomena in terms of a weakly coupled $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit $n\to1$. Taking this replica limit analytically, we derive universal signatures of the critical phase: an optimal Pauli decoding fidelity that approaches a universal function of the system's aspect ratio in the thermodynamic limit, and a dual fidelity correlator that decays as a universal power law. These observables relate to correlations of twist operators in the sigma model description. Large-scale numerical simulations confirm these analytical predictions. We also argue that the algebraic SWSSB phase cannot be realized by any Pauli dephasing channel acting on the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ paramagnet. We probe this "non-classical" character through the output state's sensitivity to well-separated $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fluxes inserted in the initial state, which reveals persistent coherence between distinct $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ charge trajectories at long distances.</summary>

    <title>Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:42:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40565v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40565v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics</summary>

    <title>Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:42:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40564v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40564v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.</summary>

    <summary>This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization.     <title>Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:41:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40561v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40561v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.</summary>

    <updated>2026-10-29T17:40:57Z</updated>

    <summary>Automated computational science could accelerate discovery by selecting, adapting and developing numerical methods. This prospect requires mathematical knowledge that AI systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. Here we present FARMS, a faithful and efficient foundation that transforms computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge. FARMS connects formal statements to source context, algorithmic meaning and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations and semantic review. Across 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline, with mean estimated costs of US \$0.85-2.29 per target across sources. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises connect selected statements to computational skills, illustrated by a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression. FARMS therefore supports an affordable, reusable knowledge foundation for trustworthy automated computational science.</summary>

    <summary>Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings.     <summary>As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.</summary>

    <title>Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:37:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40545v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40545v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.</summary>

* Written informed consent and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) authorization
* Participants must have histologically confirmed B-cell CLL, including small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), DLBCL, MCL, or FL
* B-cell NHL: a) Have previous confirmation of B-cell NHL b) Participants with DLBCL or MCL, must have relapsed or refractory disease after at least one prior regimen containing rituximab, either alone or in combination, and be ineligible for any available standard line of therapy known to be life-prolonging or life-saving c) Participants with FL, must have relapsed or refractory disease after at least two prior regimens, one of which included rituximab, either alone or in combination, and be ineligible for any available standard line of therapy known to be life-prolonging or life-saving d) Have measurable disease (at least one lesion greater than or equal to (≥) 20 millimeter (mm) in one dimension or ≥ 15 mm in two dimensions as measured by conventional or high resolution \[spiral\] computed tomography e) Not be a candidate for a hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) or bone marrow transplant
* B-cell CLL: a) Have previous confirmation of B-cell CLL with a characteristic immunophenotype by flow cytometry b) Have relapsed or refractory disease after at least 2 prior lines of treatment, at least 1 of which must have contained rituximab and be ineligible for any available standard line of therapy known to be life-prolonging or life-saving c) Not be a candidate for an HSC or BM transplant d) Have symptomatic disease that requires treatment
* Karnofsky Performance Status ≥ 70
* Life expectancy of ≥ 12 weeks
* Toxicities from previous cancer therapies must have recovered to Grade less than (\<) 2
* Adequate hematological function defined as: a) Hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL b) Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1500/mm\^3 c) Platelet count ≥ 75,000/mm\^3
* Prothrombin time-International Normalized Ratio/Partial thromboplastin time less than or equal to (≤) 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN), or for participants on anticoagulation therapy, status within therapeutic range
* Women of non-child-bearing potential or using effective contraception
* Male participants with partners of child-bearing potential must be surgically sterile or use a contraceptive method

* Any available standard line of therapy known to be life-prolonging or life-saving

1. Documented primary diagnosis of histologic- or cytologic-confirmed solid tumor cancer inclusive of gastric adenocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), breast cancer, angiosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and alveolar soft part sarcoma or other solid tumor for which anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR)2 targeted therapy could be applicable.
2. Locally advanced unresectable or metastatic disease.
3. Nivolumab treatment naive and able to begin nivolumab treatment concurrently with initiation of apatinib or have received at least 3 doses of nivolumab treatment and are continuing nivolumab therapy.
4. 1 or more measurable lesions per RECIST v1.1.
5. Participants who have adequate bone-marrow, renal and liver function including:

   1. Hematologic: absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1,500/ cubic millimetre (mm\^3), platelets≥ 100,000/mm\^3, hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 grams (g)/ per decilitre (dL) (blood transfusion to meet the inclusion criteria within 2 weeks is not allowed).
   2. Renal: serum creatinine \< 1.5× upper limit of normal (ULN); urinary protein should be\< 2+ on dipstick or routine urinalysis. If urine dipstick or routine analysis indicates proteinuria ≥ 2+, then a 24-hour urine or urine protein/creatinine ratio must be collected and must demonstrate \<2 g of protein in 24 hours to allow participation in the study.
   3. Hepatic: serum bilirubin \< 1.5× ULN, aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) ≤ 3.0× ULN(≤ 4.0× ULN, if with liver metastases).
   4. Blood coagulation tests: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and international normalized ratio (INR) ≤ 1.5× ULN and ≤ 1.5×ULN, respectively.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status are evaluated to be ≤ 1 (Participants with ECOG performance status of 2 may be enrolled only with advance review and written approval by the medical monitor).
7. Expected survival of ≥ 12 weeks, in the judgement of the investigator.
8. Ability to swallow the study drug tablets.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. History of another malignancy within 2 years prior to enrollment, unless it does not pose a significant risk to life expectancy as per the investigator.
2. Central nervous system (CNS) metastases as shown by radiology records or clinical evidence of symptomatic CNS involvement in the last 3 months prior to enrollment. Participants are eligible if metastases have been treated and have returned to neurologic baseline or are neurologically stable (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment).
3. Cytotoxic chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy or other targeted therapies and checkpoint inhibitors (excluding nivolumab if not nivolumab treatment naive) within 3 weeks (4 weeks in cases of ramucirumab, mitomycin C, nitrosourea, lomustine; 1 week in case of biopsy) prior to enrollment (adjuvant radiotherapy given to local area for non-curative symptom relief is allowed until 2 weeks before enrollment).
4. Any other therapies including biological and approved therapies within 3 half-lives or 3 weeks whichever is longer and have not recovered from all toxicities from the treatment.
5. Therapy with clinically significant systemic anticoagulant or anti thrombotic agents within 7 days prior to enrollment that may prevent blood clotting and, in the investigator's opinion, could place the participants at risk. Maximum dose of 325 milligram (mg)/day of aspirin is allowed.
6. History of bleeding diathesis or clinically significant bleeding within 14 days prior to enrollment.
7. History of clinically significant thrombosis (bleeding or clotting disorder) within the past 3 months prior to enrollment that, in the investigator's opinion, may place the participant at risk of side effects from anti-angiogenesis products.
8. History of gastrointestinal bleeding, gastric stress ulcerations, or peptic ulcer disease within the past 3 months prior to enrollment that, in the investigator's opinion, may place the participant at risk of side effects from anti-angiogenesis products.
9. Myocardial infarction or an unstable angina pectoris within 3 months prior to enrollment.
10. Prior major surgery or fracture within 3 weeks prior to enrollment or presence of any non-healing wound (procedures such as catheter placement are not considered to be major).
11. Participation in any other interventional clinical trial, within 4 weeks prior to enrollment or while participating in this study.
12. Previous treatment with apatinib.
13. Hypersensitivity to apatinib or components of its formulation.
14. History of uncontrolled hypertension (\[HTN\], blood pressure ≥ 140/90 millimeters of mercury \[mmHg\]) and change in anti hypertensive medication within 7 days prior to enrollment) that is not well managed by medication and the risk of which may be precipitated by VEGF inhibitor therapy.
15. History of severe adverse events including uncontrolled HTN or other common anti-angiogenesis class drug effects that were related to ramucirumab or bevacizumab discontinuation and/or may indicate a higher risk to the safety of the participant if provided further anti-angiogenesis treatment, in the investigator's opinion.
16. Based on these reasons, the various difficulties experienced by CRC survivors and the lack of strong evidence in the systematic analyzes led us to conduct this study.","detailedDescription":"EFFECTS OF MINDFULNESS-BASED YOGA AND MEDITATION ON SLEEP DISORDER, FACILIATION AND QUALITY OF LIFE IN PATIENTS WITH COLORECTAL CANCER: A RANDOMIZED COMPARATIVE STUDY INTRODUCTION Colorectal cancers (CRC) are the third most common type of cancer in both men and women worldwide and are the second leading cause of death from cancer (Thanikachalam, 2019). Although the incidence and mortality of CRC have decreased thanks to early detection methods, it is estimated that 149,500 patients will be newly diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2021 and approximately 52,980 people will die from this disease (Siegel, 2021). At the same time, thanks to the advances in early diagnosis and treatment methods, an increase in cancer survival rate of approximately 60% is observed (Dunn, 2006). Therefore, there is a rapid increase in efforts to maximize the quality of life for cancer survivors and to solve ongoing problems (Ramsey, 2000; Zabora, 2021). According to the joint outcome reports of these studies on cancer survivors, it is reported that a number of psychosocial and physical problems develop during or after cancer diagnosis and treatment. In studies, the most common problems included depression and anxiety, low self-esteem and body image; treatment side effects such as fatigue, pain and nausea; decrease in cardiovascular functions and muscle weakness (Dunn, 2006; Brown, 2003; Deimling, 2002; Arndt, 2017). In addition, in the first 12 months following diagnosis, approximately 60% of CRC survivors experience problems such as overweight, 70% limitation in physical activity, and 22% alcohol dependence (Honda, 2005). In addition to these problems, it has been determined that there is an increase in cancer survival in bad lifestyle factors such as smoking and obesity (Gunnell, 2017; Friedenreich, 2016; Demark, 2008). In addition, it is estimated that 40% of post-CRC survivors struggle with psychological problems (Blanchard, 2008) and a significant proportion do not comply with current public health guidelines in terms of lifestyle factors or healthy lifestyle behaviors (Lynch, 2007; Hawkes, 2008). It is emphasized that most of them affect the quality of life of individuals negatively in all areas during their survival (Carver, 2006; Ramsey, 2000;Blanchard, 2008).

The survivors of CRC are in a different group compared to other types of cancer in that CRC is detected at more advanced stages, they are subject to different medical and surgical procedures, they are of advanced age, and they include equal numbers of men and women. (Skiber, 2001). In addition, it is stated that individuals who survive compared to other types of cancer have relatively more difficulties in maintaining a healthy lifestyle both before and after treatment. For these reasons, results from studies in different types of cancer groups may not be generalizable to colorectal cancer survivors (Skibber, 2001). Although, as a result of a randomized comparative study of lifelong interventions for cancer survivors in different types of cancer groups, it is emphasized that the implementation of various interventions positively affects health (Courneya, 2003). In particular, it is suggested that these interventions in the period immediately after diagnosis and treatment will be much more effective (Demark, 2005; Doyle, 2006; Demark, 2008). Because the period immediately after cancer diagnosis and treatment has been defined as the "teachable period". Despite the difficulties of cancer diagnosis and treatment, it was determined that the individuals who survived this period had high levels of motivation to optimize their health, prevent cancer recurrence, and make behavioral improvements (Demark, 2005; Doyle, 2006; Demark, 2008).

Yoga and meditation practices are among the most common interventions to provide physical and psychological benefits, especially to cancer survivors (Distasio, 2008). Lengacher et al. In their randomized comparative study, the mindfulness-based meditation program they applied to cancer patients reduced physical and psychological symptoms, and similarly, Bower et al. It was found that targeted yoga intervention (Bower, 2012) for breast cancer patients reduced long-lasting symptoms of fatigue and burnout and led to significant improvements in vitality. Additionally, in a review by Distasio, she mentioned the types of yoga and its potential benefits, emphasizing the importance of introducing yoga to nurses as a complementary therapy and integrating yoga into cancer care. It has also been stated that nurses can integrate yoga and meditation into cancer care by educating patients, explaining the potential benefits and risks, and discussing how to choose a program. To summarize, mindfulness-based programs for cancer survivors may have clinical potential, and according to the results of these studies mentioned above, we can say that the use of yoga and meditation practices as a complementary alternative medicine is beneficial and is becoming increasingly popular. Additionally, most studies suggest that yoga improves patients' physical and psychological symptoms, quality of life, and immune processes, providing strong support for the integration of yoga into traditional cancer care.

In many systematic reviews, it has also been emphasized that different cancer groups and a large number of applications are needed in order to obtain definitive conclusions about the effect of various interventions applied to these patients (Smith et al, 2004: Mosher et al, 2017: Fieke, 2015). In addition, in the joint results of these studies, it was stated that there are very few studies supporting the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for CRC patients, and these studies have a limited evidence base, and specifically due to the lack of strong evidence regarding the physiological and psychological difficulties of cancer treatment in the CRC patient group and the practices performed. The level of evidence needs to be strengthened with further studies. Based on these reasons, the various difficulties experienced by CRC survivors and the lack of strong evidence in the systematic analyzes led us to conduct this study.

METHOD:

Purpose of the research:

This study was planned to examine the effects of mindfulness-based yoga and meditation on sleep disturbance, fatigue and quality of life in CRC survivors.

Method of research:

The study was planned as a randomized comparative study. Place of research The study was treated in the colorectal cancer treatment unit of a private research hospital between October 2021 and March 2022; consisted of patients who met the inclusion criteria of the study. Yoga and meditation practices are held online at the participants' homes due to the covid-19 pandemic.

The universe and sample of the research The population of the study consists of approximately 200 participants who applied to the hospital within one year of the application and were diagnosed with CRC. The number of samples was determined as 90 people in total as experimental and comparison groups.

Inclusion criteria:

* Participants' consent for their physicians to participate in the study
* Being a stage 1-4 patient diagnosed with colorectal cancer,
* Being between the ages of 20-70,
* Being receiving outpatient treatment,
* At least 1 month has passed after the operation

Exclusion criteria:

* Conditions that will hinder physical activity (Hemoglobin value less than 10mg/Dl, Platelet value less than 50,000)
* Cognitive disability

Ethical Dimension:

Ethics committee approval no: 95961207-604.01.01-E.64779 for the study was obtained from Istanbul Medipol University, GETAT Clinical Research Ethics Committee and the Ministry of Health and Koç University Hospital with the date and number of 12/12/2019.

APPLICATION The application was carried out by the researcher who had completed mindfulness-based yoga and meditation training.

Randomization: In the colorectal surgery unit of the center where the research was conducted, the patients who met the criteria of the study were determined by the responsible physician and coordinator of the department, and a patient pool was created. Patients who wanted to be included in the study were listed for randomization after the patients were contacted by phone from this patient pool determined by the coordinator and they were informed about the study. Individuals from the list were divided into two groups by randomization method, while the first group was treated, the other waiting list group was included in the comparison group. (The SPSS syntax program was used to randomly select 15 participants from the eligible candidates in the file). All of the scales were applied to all individuals in the patient pool before starting the study.

For the intervention groups, 3 intervention groups of 15 people (45 people in total) were formed. The other 45 people on the waiting list formed the comparison group. The program to be implemented in intervention groups is designed as 2 modules. In the first module of this designed program, a mindfulness-based yoga module was planned for a total of 8 weeks (once a week, each section lasting 60 minutes). The mindfulness-based meditation section of the Second Module consisted of sections that lasted 30 minutes once a week for 8 weeks in total.

INITIATIVES:

Comparison group:

Patients in the comparison group will not be subjected to any intervention other than the tests specified in the method. Comparison group patients will continue their standard treatment and care. Questionnaires and scales will be applied to this group again before the application starts and after the application is finished.

Intervention group:

For this study, a yoga exercise and mindfulness program suitable for colorectal cancer patients was designed with a trainer who has yoga and meditation training. The program consists of two modules. In this designed program, the yoga exercises module, which is the first module, is planned for a total of 8 weeks, once a week, and each section will last 60 minutes. The first 15 minutes of the program consist of meditation and pranamaya (breathing exercise), 30 minutes of asana (physical movements and stretching), and 15 minutes of savasana (relaxation) (Table 1). The second module of the program is the meditation section under the guidance of mindfulness. The meditation section is also 8 weeks in total. It is to be applied once a week and each section consists of sections lasting 30 minutes (Table 2). To summarize, patients in the intervention group will attend two sessions per week, one yoga session and one meditation session.   * Min # of sessions: whole breast: 22 Gy; breast boost: 5 Gy; tumor bed = whole breast +/- boost: 25 Gy; lymph nodes: 25 Gy
  * Max # of sessions: whole breast: 28 Gy; breast boost: 10 Gy; tumor bed = whole breast +/- boost: 36 Gy; lymph nodes: 28 Gy
* Subjects may or may not have had surgery (lumpectomy or mastectomy) prior to RT; (NOTE: surgery is not required for eligibility)

* Previous diagnosis of collagen vascular disorder or vasculitis

1. Patients with CD20 positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma as confirmed by a pathological biopsy report.
2. Patients who are candidates for autologous stem-cell transplantation due to primary refractory or first relapse of disease.
3. Patients must have chemo-sensitive disease achieving at least partial response (Cheson 2007 criteria) to last chemotherapy.
4. Patients with adequate autologous stem cell collection for transplantation (target \>= 2.5 x 10\^6 CD34+ cells/kg).
5. Patients must sign written informed consent.
6. Adequate birth control in fertile patients.
7. All prior chemotherapy completed at least three weeks before study treatment.
8. Marrow involvement less than 25% at transplantation, no limitation on blood counts (low platelet count allowed).
9. Negative HIV antibody.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Chemo-refractory disease as determined by less than partial response (Cheson 2007 Criteria) to last chemotherapy.
2. Two or more relapses after initial response to induction chemotherapy.
3. High-grade transformation from earlier diagnosis of low-grade lymphoma. Patients with "De Novo" Transformed DLBCL, defined as DLBCL only on lymph node biopsy and a discordant marrow with para-trabecular small cells at first diagnosis of lymphoma, are eligible if adherent to all other selection criteria.
4. Bilirubin \> 3.0 mg/dl, transaminases \> 3 times upper normal limit.
5. Creatinine \> 2.0 mg/dl.
6. KPS \< 70.
7. Uncontrolled infection.
8. Pregnancy or lactation.
9. Abnormal lung diffusion capacity (DLCO \< 40% predicted).
10. Severe cardiovascular disease; New York Heart Association (NYHA) Functional Classification ≥2.
11. Active CNS disease involvement.
12. Presence of any other malignancy or history of prior malignancy within 5 years of study entry. Within 5 years, patients treated for Stage I or II cancers are eligible provided they have a life expectancy \> 5 years in relation to this prior malignance. The 5-year exclusion rule does not apply to-non melanoma skin tumors and in situ cervical cancer.
13. Pleural effusion or ascites \> 1 liter.
14. Known hypersensitivity to rituximab.
15. Psychiatric conditions/disease that impair the ability to give informed consent or to adequately co-operate.
16. Prior radioimmunotherapy.
17. Prior autologous or allogeneic HSCT.
18. Active evidence of Hepatitis B or C infection; Hepatitis B surface antigen positive.
19. Patients who have had prior radiation to the lung will be excluded from the study, although mediastinal irradiation will be permitted if minimal lung is in the treatment volume.
20.
